host.instance: AWS EC2 m7i.xlarge, 4 vCPU, 16 GiB, us-east-2
host.note: one engine on the box, one worker at a time; Python and TypeScript phases separated by idle gaps and each preceded by a 90s settle

workloads.fibonacci_40_10: one workflow, 40 sequential tasks, each naive-recursive fibo(10)
workloads.fibonacci_10_33: one workflow, 10 sequential tasks, each naive-recursive fibo(33)

method.reps: 1 discarded warmup + 5 measured reps per (language, workload), back to back
method.worker: one worker, default slot count; only one worker connected at a time
method.timings: created_at <- v1_tasks_olap.inserted_at; started_at <- max(STARTED) and completed_at <- max(FINISHED) in v1_task_events_olap; one task per run cross-checked against GET /api/v1/stable/tasks/{id} (all agreed within 0.5ms)
method.order: python 40x10, python 10x33, typescript 40x10, typescript 10x33, then a python 40x10 control re-run (control_hatchet_py_fibonacci_40_10.json) to check for order effects

caveats: In the TypeScript runs the task body is synchronous, so it blocks the Node event loop and the SDK flushes its STARTED event only after the function returns. On fibonacci_10_33 that puts the ~31ms of compute inside the created->started window and collapses completed_at-started_at to ~1ms. created_at and completed_at, and therefore every total and per-task figure here, are unaffected; started_at is not a usable dispatch timestamp for the TypeScript 10x33 rows.

fibo(33) is ~10x faster in Node than in CPython, so raw totals on fibonacci_10_33 are not comparable across the two languages. Compare overhead per task (median total minus measured compute, divided by task count).
The hatchet-lite v0.107.0 python:3.12-slim worker image now resolves to CPython 3.12.15; the September 2026 run recorded 3.12.14.
Hatchet's per-task latency is not stationary (the documented setup notes degradation under sustained load), hence the 90s settle before each phase and the >=120s idle gaps between them.
